Title: Android malware detection applying feature selection techniques and machine learning
High_Level_Domains: Mobile Security; Machine Learning; Android Security
Core_Techniques: Machine Learning; Feature Selection; Ensemble Learning
Specific_Algorithms_Models: Random Forest; effective feature selection; high weight feature selection; effective group feature selection
Feature_Representation: Feature vectors based on: hardware components; requested permissions; filtered intents; restricted API calls; used permissions; suspicious API calls
Feature_Engineering_Steps: Effective feature selection (based on difference in usage between malware and benign apps); High weight feature selection (based on feature importance from an initial RF run); Effective group feature selection (based on differences in feature group usage)
Data_Preprocessing_Steps: Reverse engineering of APK files; Feature extraction; Feature selection
Dataset_Composition: 123,453 real applications; 5560 malware instances from 179 types
Evaluation_Metrics: Accuracy (ACC); False Positive Ratio (FPR); False Negative Ratio (FNR); True Positive Ratio (TPR); True Negative Ratio (TNR); Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC); F-measure; Required Time
Baselines_Compared_Against: k-nearest neighbours (k=1, k=3, k=5); Simple Logistic (SL); Naïve Bayes (NB); Decision tree (J48); Random Tree (RT); Random Forest (with 10, 50, and 100 trees); PIndroid; SensDroid; RNPDroid
Reported_Performance_Summary: The proposed RF-EF model achieved an accuracy of 0.9949, an F-measure of 0.939, and an AUC of 0.956. It significantly reduced the required time compared to standard RF (72s vs 2159s) and outperformed most baselines in terms of accuracy and F-measure.
Stated_Contributions: Application of three feature selection strategies (effective, high weight, and effective group) as a pre-processing step for a Random Forest malware detector.
Stated_Limitations: The selected features in the RF-EF model showed some sensitiveness that tended to misclassify real applications as malicious, resulting in a higher FNR compared to some baselines.
Future_Work_Ideas: Embedding feature selection within the learning model itself.
Reviewer_Notes: The paper proposes combining Random Forest with one of three feature selection techniques. The 'effective feature selection' (EF) method, which selects features based on the difference in usage between malware and benign apps, performed best. The main benefit was a massive reduction in computation time with a slight improvement in detection metrics. The comparison with baselines is extensive.

Title: Trojan Detection Test for Clockless Circuits
Authors: Ricardo Aquino Guazzelli; Matheus Garay Trindade; Leonel Acunha Guimara˜es; Thiago Ferreira de Paiva Leite; Laurent Fesquet; Rodrigo Possamai Bastos
Primary_Problem: Hardware Trojan (HT) detection in clockless (asynchronous) circuits
Secondary_Problems: Side-channel analysis; Differentiating HT effects from process variations (PV); Applying machine learning for classification
High_Level_Domains: Hardware Security; Integrated Circuit (IC) Design; Machine Learning
Core_Techniques: Current Signature Analysis; Machine Learning Classification
Specific_Algorithms_Models: One-Class Support Vector Machine (OC-SVM); Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
Feature_Representation: Points of the transient current (Iddt) signature curve
Feature_Engineering_Steps: Partitioning the global current signature (Iddt) into individual signatures corresponding to different pipeline stages; Using current signatures from multiple supply voltages (voltage scaling)
Data_Preprocessing_Steps: Partitioning current signatures based on pipeline stage propagation delay
Datasets_Used: Simulated data from an 8-bit QDI asynchronous ALU design
Dataset_Composition: Golden DUTT samples: 400 Monte Carlo (MC) simulations of a Trojan-free ALU. Trojan-infected DUTT samples: 50 MC simulations for each of 24 HT test cases (total 1200 MC simulations). Seven comparator-based Trojans and one pass-transistor-based Trojan were used.
Reported_Performance_Summary: Achieved 100% detection accuracy for all comparator-based HTs (down to 34 transistors), an improvement over a previous technique [19] which had 77.67% accuracy for a 102-transistor HT. Detection accuracy for a smaller 30-transistor pass-transistor-based HT is lower and shows a trade-off with the number of training samples.
Stated_Contributions: A testing technique to detect HTs in clockless circuits using One-Class SVM on current signatures; Demonstrates the natural ability of clockless circuits to provide individual current signatures for HT identification; The technique requires no extra circuitry or power ports; The technique can detect HTs of a few dozen transistors in a design with over 13 thousand transistors.
Stated_Limitations: The technique requires a set of certified golden (Trojan-free) DUTT samples for training; There is a trade-off between Trojan-free classification accuracy and the detection accuracy for very small/furtive HTs (e.g., pass-transistor-based Trojans).
Future_Work_Ideas: Exploring the automated generation of the stimulus procedure; Adapting the proposed technique to allow HT detection without the assumption of existence of fabricated devices as golden references.
Reviewer_Notes: The paper presents a novel method for detecting Hardware Trojans in clockless (QDI asynchronous) circuits. It leverages the intrinsic properties of these circuits, where different pipeline stages are active at different times, to isolate current signatures. By applying a One-Class SVM to these signatures, the method achieves high detection accuracy for small Trojans without needing extra hardware. The main novelty lies in using the entire current signature shape as features for the OC-SVM, combined with voltage scaling, which proves more effective than prior methods that only used peaks and delays. The reliance on golden samples is a key assumption.
